summary: Specifies the Java bindings for the Generic Security Service API, which RFC 2743 describes in a language-independent way. It is on the standards track and was replaced by RFC 5653.

plainLanguage.summary: A security toolkit described in general words is turned into specific instructions for programmers who write Java.

questions: how do java programs use kerberos
how to protect messages in java
subtitle: How Java programs use cryptographic security services

tldr.problem: Application programmers need a uniform way to use security services like authentication and encryption from different underlying cryptographic systems.
tldr.mechanism: GSS-API is defined in language-independent terms in RFC 2743; this RFC translates it into specific Java classes, interfaces and methods.
tldr.outcome: Java programs can use Kerberos, public-key systems and other mechanisms through one consistent set of classes. RFC 5653 updated this specification.

today: RFC 2853 was a Proposed Standard. It was updated and replaced by RFC 5653 in 2009, which adjusted the API based on implementation experience.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
This document specifies the Generic Security Service API Version 2 (GSS-API) as a set of Java classes and interfaces. GSS-API itself is described in language-independent terms in RFC 2743.

The GSS-API lets an application authenticate a user, delegate rights to another application, and protect messages by adding integrity protection and encryption. Underlying mechanisms like Kerberos or public-key systems handle the cryptography; the Java API hides the differences so applications can switch mechanisms without changing code.

The API supports both system-wide implementations (libraries all applications can use) and custom implementations bundled with a single application. It leverages Java's provider framework so new mechanisms can be added at runtime.
sections.plainLanguage: A toolkit for security is described in general words in one RFC. This RFC turns those general words into actual Java code that programmers can use.

sections.title: How GSS-API Works
sections.content:
GSS-API follows a four-stage process. First, an application acquires credentials that prove its identity to other applications. Second, two applications establish a security context using their credentials. This context holds shared state like cryptographic keys and message sequence numbers. Third, once the context is established, the application can protect individual messages using either getMIC (to add a cryptographic checksum) or wrap (to encrypt and protect a message). Fourth, when communication ends, the context is closed and resources are released.

A GSSContext object represents the shared security state. When methods like initSecContext or acceptSecContext are called, they generate tokens (cryptographically protected opaque data) that the caller must send to the peer, who passes them to corresponding methods on their own GSSContext to update the shared state.
sections.plainLanguage: Two programs have a secret handshake to prove who they are. Once they agree on shared secrets, they can pass protected messages back and forth. When they are done, they forget the secrets.

sections.title: Optional Security Services
sections.content:
Before establishing a context, the initiator can request optional services. Delegation allows the initiator to give the acceptor permission to act on its behalf, so the acceptor can establish new contexts as an agent of the initiator. Mutual authentication means the acceptor also proves its identity back to the initiator. Replay and out-of-sequence detection let the API detect if messages are duplicated or received in the wrong order, by numbering and sequencing them. Anonymous authentication hides the initiator's identity from the acceptor. Confidentiality means messages are encrypted, not just protected from tampering.

Not all mechanisms support all services, and some services may require others to be enabled. The context provides query methods to let the application check which services are available after establishment.
sections.plainLanguage: Before talking securely, you can ask for extras like hiding who you are, or making sure messages arrive in order.

sections.title: Core Classes and Interfaces
sections.content:
The API defines these main classes in the org.ietf.jgss package. GSSManager is a factory that creates the other objects. GSSName represents a principal (a user or service). GSSCredential holds the cryptographic data that proves a principal's identity and supports both initiating and accepting security contexts. GSSContext encapsulates the shared state needed for per-message protection. MessageProp holds properties of individual protected messages, like whether they were encrypted or detected as old or out-of-sequence. Oid represents Object Identifiers used to name mechanisms and name formats. ChannelBinding binds the security context to a lower-level communication channel. GSSException reports errors.

All classes use Java's automatic memory management, eliminating memory and resource management functions that the C bindings require.
sections.plainLanguage: The toolkit has a manager that makes all the pieces, names for who you are, proof of identity, the protected conversation itself, and ways to describe what happened to each message.

sections.title: Credentials and Security Context
sections.content:
A GSSCredential object contains mechanism-specific credential elements, one per mechanism. Each element holds authentication data for both context initiation and context acceptance. Credentials can be used for initiating contexts only, accepting only, or both. When no credential is passed to context creation, the application acts as a default principal.

A GSSContext is established by the initiator calling initSecContext and the acceptor calling acceptSecContext, exchanging tokens until isEstablished() returns true. Once established, the context's wrap and getMIC methods protect outgoing messages, and unwrap and verifyMIC verify incoming messages. The context can be exported to another process and re-imported there, enabling server designs where a parent process accepts contexts and passes them to child processes for data handling.
sections.plainLanguage: Credentials are your ID card. A context is the locked conversation between two programs. Once locked, you can pass protected messages through it.

sections.title: Provider Framework and Security Manager
sections.content:
GSS-API leverages Java's security provider architecture. Providers are pluggable implementations of security mechanisms. The GSSManager can work with system-wide providers (registered in the JRE) or instance-specific providers passed to it at runtime. This lets applications use custom implementations without global system changes.

When a Java Security Manager (such as browser sandboxes) is active, GSS providers operate under fine-grained access control. Administrators grant permissions through policy files. For example, a Kerberos provider that needs to contact a KDC requires network permission. Applications can add providers to a specific GSSManager instance without requiring administrative permission to modify system-wide settings.
sections.plainLanguage: The toolkit can plug in different security engines. It asks the system for permission before doing things like contacting servers for authentication.
